segments.say: This is the orchestrator we wrote at the end of the last lecture, copied into a repository it has never seen. Eighty-two lines. A list of tasks, one query per task, all of them fired at once, and a report at the end. And the verdict we recorded on it was not flattering: good at cheap, isolated, read-then-write work, and unable to edit an existing file or run a test. Both of those are about to matter, because a thing that cannot edit a file and cannot run a test cannot build a product. And notice what copying it here does, which is the thing a plugin or a package would also have done: it makes the tool travel. Eighty-two lines in a file is the smallest possible unit of a way of working, and it moved between two projects with one copy command and no install step. And there is one more thing worth noticing about copying a tool into a new repository, which is what it does not bring with it. It has no memory of the other project. It does not know what Control Tower was, or which of its tasks worked. Everything it will do here comes from this repository's plan and this repository's memory file. A tool that carried context between projects would be worse, not better.

So read this instruction, because it is a specification and not a wish, and almost none of it is about orchestration. Three phases, each runnable on its own from the command line. Plan: one agent reads the plan file and writes a task list - an id, the area it belongs to, the files it owns, the tools it is allowed, what it depends on, and a brief written for somebody who cannot ask a question. Run: execute that list respecting the dependencies, at most three at once, each in its own session with only its own tools, appending a line to a log every time a task starts, finishes or fails. Review: one agent with read-only tools inspects what was built against the plan and writes down what is present, what is missing and what is wrong. Read the three phases against each other and notice they are three different kinds of job. Planning is reading comprehension with a schema on the end. Running is scheduling, and there is no model in it at all beyond the agents it starts. Reviewing is reading comprehension again, in the opposite direction. Splitting them is not tidiness - it means each one can be run on its own, which is what you need at four in the afternoon when the build is fine and the review was wrong. And read what each phase is allowed to touch, because that is a design decision and not a detail. The planner can read and write, but the only file it writes is the task list. The reviewer can read and write, and the only file it writes is the review. Only the jobs inside the run phase get to touch the product, and each of those gets the tools its own brief names. Three phases, three different blast radiuses, all set in one file you can see at once.

Three things in there are doing all the work, and they are worth naming separately because you will want all three in anything you build like this. The dependency list, because without it the server starts before the simulator exists and builds against a guess. The per-task tool grant, because that is the only thing standing between an unattended run and a bad afternoon - there is no permission prompt anywhere in this design, deliberately, since there is nobody to answer one. And the log, because when you come back to a finished repository the log is the only account of what happened that you did not have to take on trust. Two clauses at the end of that instruction exist because nobody will be in the room. Do not ask me any questions: if a choice comes up, make it and say why. And if evidence for something is missing, say so rather than guessing. An agent that stops to ask is a stopped build; one that guesses is worse. There is a fourth thing that is not in the instruction, and its absence is deliberate: no retry. If a job fails, it fails, and the jobs that depended on it are skipped rather than run against nothing. Retries feel like robustness and are usually the opposite - they turn one clear failure into three unclear ones and a bill. If a job failed because its brief was wrong, running it again produces the same result more expensively. And there is a question worth asking before you write any of this, which is whether you need it at all. If your work is a list of independent jobs that each read something and write something new, the eighty-two line version does it and you can stop. What buys you the other three hundred lines is dependencies - the moment one job's output is another job's input, you need ordering, and once you need ordering you need to decide what happens when something upstream fails. That is the whole of the difference. And the reason a task list is a file rather than a function call is worth one sentence, because it is the decision that makes the whole thing debuggable. You can read it. You can edit it. You can delete one task and run the rest. When something goes wrong at task five, the thing you want most is to run task five again on its own, and that is only possible because the plan phase wrote its decision down instead of acting on it.

And then the last clause, which is not about behaviour at all: keep it one file and keep it readable, because this is a tool a person has to be able to debug at two in the morning. I want to be specific about why that is in there. Everything else in this instruction describes what the program does. That clause describes what happens when it does something else. A three-hundred-line file you can read start to finish is one afternoon of debugging. The same behaviour spread across a plugin system and four abstractions is a week, and the agent will happily build you either. And there is a second reason to insist on one readable file, which is about what you are actually buying here. There are orchestrators you can install. Some of them are good. But the moment the interesting question becomes why did it run those two in parallel, you are reading somebody else's source anyway - and theirs is ten thousand lines and yours is three hundred. The argument for writing your own is not that it is better. It is that you can answer questions about it. There is a second half to that clause that is easy to miss, which is who it has to be readable for. Not you today, while the whole design is still in your head. You in three weeks, or whoever inherits this while you are away, opening a file they have never seen because something failed overnight. That reader has no context, and every abstraction you did not need is another room they have to walk through before they reach the thing that broke. And there is a cheap test for whether a constraint like this one is real: ask what you would have to give up to satisfy it. Readable and one file costs almost nothing here, because the program genuinely is small. If satisfying it were expensive, the constraint would be the wrong one, and the honest move would be to change it rather than quietly ignore it. There is a version of that clause I have seen produce much worse results, which is make it production ready. That phrase means nothing to a person and even less to a model, and what comes back is layers: a config file, an abstraction over the SDK, a plugin point for future backends. All of it reasonable, none of it asked for, and every line of it something you now own. Readable and one file is a constraint. Production ready is a mood.

So it works, and again the correct thing to do here is nothing. But it is worth watching what it does before it writes, because it is the same pattern from the last lecture: it goes and reads the package it is about to write against rather than remembering it. That habit is worth more than any particular thing in this file. The Agent SDK is new and it is moving, and anything written about it more than a couple of months ago describes option names that may not exist any more. A model answering from memory here is answering from a snapshot of a moving target. A model that opens the package on your disk is answering from the version you are actually about to run. Watch what it does before it writes, though, because it repeats the pattern from Friday and it is the habit worth stealing. It checks the repository layout. It installs the package. And then it opens the package's own type definitions on disk and reads them, so that it is not guessing at option names. And it is worth being clear about what that habit protects you from, because it is not embarrassment. A wrong option name usually does not throw. It gets ignored, and the run proceeds with a default you did not choose - a different model, no tool restriction, a permission mode that stops and waits. You find out from the bill, or from a build that hung overnight, not from an error. There is one more thing in what it reads that is easy to miss. It opens the type definitions, which are a description of the library's shape, not its behaviour. Watch what it puts at the bottom of the file: a command line that takes plan, run, review or all, so each phase can be run on its own. That is the three runnable phases, in twenty lines of argument parsing. Then it does something nobody asked for. It runs node dash dash check on what it wrote, then exercises the scheduler against a synthetic task list with a fake agent standing in for the real one, so concurrency, dependency gating and cascading skip get tested without a single call to the API. Testing an orchestrator by running it is expensive. Testing it with the expensive part taken out is not. That is enough to get the option names right and not enough to get the semantics right - and the difference between those two is where the remaining bugs in a file like this live.

And while this runs, here is the question I would want you asking, because it is the one this lecture is really about. Why write this at all, when there are orchestrators you can install. Six minutes thirty-nine, thirty thousand tokens, and it is still proving to itself that the scheduler cannot deadlock. The answer is not that ours is better. It is that in about six minutes you will be able to read every line of the thing that is running six agents in your repository, and change any of it, and you will never again be in a position where the only way to coordinate agents is a tool somebody else ships you and can stop shipping. And the honest counterweight to that, which I would rather say than have you discover: what you are giving up is everything a mature orchestrator has that this does not. No resumable runs, so a failure at minute fifteen means starting again. No isolation between workers beyond the tool list. No verification pass built in - we are writing ours as a third phase because it is not there. Every one of those is a day's work you have signed up for, on the day you need it. The other honest answer is that ours is not competing with theirs. What we are building is the smallest thing that runs this plan, in a file the student can read in a coffee break, so that the idea of an orchestrator stops being a product category and becomes a thing you know the shape of. If you later install somebody else's, you will read its documentation completely differently - you will know which of its features are the essential forty lines and which are the day you have not had yet. And there is a question underneath this whole lecture that I want to leave you with rather than answer, because the answer depends on you. The thing we are building can run six agents unattended in a repository. That is a capability, and capabilities do not come with judgement attached.

Three hundred and sixty-six lines, from eighty-two. And read down it, because almost none of that growth is orchestration. At the top, two constants: the model, named once, and a maximum of three agents at a time. Then the function that runs one agent - and the comment above it is the most important thing in the file. Permissions are bypassed deliberately, because this pipeline has no human to answer a prompt, so each task's safety comes from its tool list being scoped to what that task needs rather than from a dialog somebody would have dismissed anyway. That is the trade, written down, where the next person will find it. Sixty-six lines of that growth are the validator alone, and none of it is the interesting part - which is exactly the point. The orchestration in here is about forty lines.

Then a validator, which nobody asked for. It checks that every task has the fields it needs, that every dependency names a task that exists, and that the graph has no cycle in it - and if any of that fails it refuses to start rather than running half a build. Then the scheduler, and it is about thirty lines. A task whose dependencies are done becomes eligible. A task whose dependency failed is not run at all: it is marked skipped, with the reason written to the log, because building the server against a simulator that was never built produces something worse than nothing. And a check for the case where nothing is running and nothing can start, which throws instead of spinning forever. The skip rule is the one I would argue for hardest if somebody wanted to take it out.

And one dependency, which is not part of the application. The memory file this repository wrote for itself says zero dependencies for the running app, and that rule is about to be bent in exactly the way it was bent in the other project: the orchestrator is a development tool, not part of the thing that ships, and the console still starts with no network and nothing beyond Node. Remember that this is not written down here yet.
